rows.prerequisites: ORS 305.992 and OAR 150-305-0068 (waived on written request before full payment or within a year after: 70% filed before any notice, 50% after a demand, 25% after an assessment), as content/statetax.ts carries them. A penalty already paid and then waived is an overpayment the department credits to what's owed or refunds (SLATE's reading of ORS 314.415's refunds and credits; the waiver's own text says nothing of a part already paid).
rows.reads: Unreachable: only Oregon charges it (content/statetax.ts, us-or threeYear) and every life files in Connecticut (played: tests/scope-taxpapers.test.ts). Retained engine at 25% only (tests/liens-and-arrangements.test.ts:259). promises.claim: Filing takes any balance from your accounts at once, the checking account first and then savings.
Filing answers the year’s item in What Needs You.
A balance your bank couldn’t pay at filing stays owed: the IRS’s bill comes at once, and its first reminder ${said(COLLECTION.noticeWeeks)} weeks after the deadline, or after filing if that’s later.
A refund is paid into your checking account ${RETURN.refundDays} days after filing, or ${ITIN_REFUND_DAYS} days on a 1040-NR filed without a Social Security number.
The Papers line on Home says when an unfiled return is due, what filing it would pay (including any late penalty), and the tax you owe.
On a 1040-NR, having a Social Security number before you file saves the ${said(SSN.itinWeeks)} weeks an ITIN application holds up the refund.
You owe a balance only on a filed return, or on one the IRS or a state assessed without you.
Each payment leaves your accounts at once, the checking account first and then savings.
Paying a year in full moves its lien to Paid: Release To Come.
If you leave it owing, a levy takes what your accounts hold on its day.
Tax owed weighs on you: each day ends with more stress and less morale until it’s paid.
When you can’t pay at once, a plan stops collection for as long as you keep it up.
Every return past its due date has to be filed before the IRS or a state sets up a plan.
A plan being decided or in force stops the letters and the levy on what you owe.
While a state plan is in force, no lien is filed, and one that was only announced comes to nothing.
Each plan payment is taken from your accounts on its day, every 30 days.
A Social Security number gets an IRS plan decided within a minute. Without one it takes ${PLAN.mailDays} days.
A lien is released only once what it was filed for is paid in full.
A lien is withdrawn as filed in error only after your own return has replaced the assessment it was filed on.
While a state plan is in force, no lien is filed. Connecticut files its lien at its second notice.
